# Recession modes for bounded-diameter fibers over a fixed integer projection

This note identifies the exact linear recession space and the finite graph
seen after a diverging shear-normalized family is contracted. It proves a
weighted Helly bound on that graph. It does **not** transfer that bound,
or (OC), back across the collapse.

## 1. Definitions and equivalent finite descriptions

Let \(P\subset\mathbb Z^n\) be nonempty and finite, with
\(P=\operatorname{conv}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^n\). Write
\(Q=\operatorname{conv}(P)\), \(N=|P|\), and \(r=\dim Q\).
All interiors and dimensions of faces below are relative to their affine
hulls. Let \(\mathcal A(P)\subset\mathbb R^P\) denote the restrictions to
\(P\) of ordinary affine functions on \(\mathbb R^n\); it has dimension
\(r+1\).

Define \(\mathcal L(P)\) to consist of the scalar functions \(g:P\to\mathbb R\)
such that
\[
 \sum_{w\in P}\lambda_w w=z,\quad
 \lambda_w\ge0,\quad\sum_w\lambda_w=1,\quad z\in P
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \sum_w\lambda_w g(w)=g(z). \tag{1}
\]
This is a linear subspace containing \(\mathcal A(P)\).

For \(z\in P\), let \(F_z\) be the minimal face of \(Q\) containing \(z\).
Equivalently, \(z\in\operatorname{relint}F_z\). Call a face \(F\)
integer-anchored if \(P\cap\operatorname{relint}F\ne\varnothing\).
Vertices are included among these faces.

**Lemma 1 (face characterization).** The following are equivalent:

1. \(g\in\mathcal L(P)\).
2. For every \(z\in P\), the restriction of \(g\) to \(P\cap F_z\) is affine.
3. For every integer-anchored face \(F\), the restriction to \(P\cap F\)
   is affine.
4. The condition in item 3 holds for the inclusion-maximal
   integer-anchored faces.

*Proof.* Suppose (1), fix an integer-anchored face \(F\), and choose
\(z\in P\cap\operatorname{relint}F\). There is a convex representation
\(z=\sum_{w\in P\cap F}\rho_w w\) with every \(\rho_w>0\).
To obtain one, take the average \(\bar w\) of \(P\cap F\). For sufficiently
small \(t>0\), relative interior gives
\(z=t\bar w+(1-t)y\) for some \(y\in F\). Expanding \(y\) as a convex
combination and adding \(t/|P\cap F|\) to every coefficient gives the
required positive representation.

For any affine dependence \(a=(a_w)\) on \(P\cap F\), namely
\(\sum a_w=0\) and \(\sum a_w w=0\), both \(\rho+\varepsilon a\) and
\(\rho-\varepsilon a\) are nonnegative representations of \(z\) when
\(\varepsilon>0\) is sufficiently small. Applying (1) and subtracting
gives \(\sum a_w g(w)=0\). Thus \(g\) annihilates every affine dependence
on \(P\cap F\). Choose an affine basis of \(F\); the unique affine
function matching \(g\) on that basis must then match it on each other
point, by the dependence expressing that point in the basis. This proves
item 3.

Item 3 implies item 2. Conversely, every positive-weight source point in
a convex representation of \(z\) lies in \(F_z\). Indeed an exposing
functional for this face has its maximum at \(z\), and an average can
attain that maximum only when each positive-weight term does. Applying
the affine restriction in item 2 to this representation proves (1).
Finally every integer-anchored face is contained in a maximal one, so
items 3 and 4 are equivalent. This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

Here is an explicit finite matrix for this space. For each maximal
integer-anchored face \(F\), choose an affine basis
\(b_0,\ldots,b_{\dim F}\) from \(P\cap F\). For each remaining
\(w\in P\cap F\), compute its affine coordinates \(t_i(w)\) in that basis
and impose
\[
 g(w)-\sum_i t_i(w)g(b_i)=0. \tag{2}
\]
If \(D_P\) is the matrix of these equations, then
\[
 \mathcal L(P)=\ker D_P,\qquad
 \dim\mathcal L(P)=N-\operatorname{rank}D_P. \tag{3}
\]
The matrix is rational and can be made integral by clearing denominators.
Equations on overlapping faces may be dependent; the rank in (3), not
the raw number of rows, gives the dimension.

An alternative matrix, useful for estimates, uses convex representations.
For each \(z\in P\), the representation polytope
\[
 R_z=\{\lambda\ge0:\sum\lambda_w=1,\ \sum\lambda_w w=z\}
\]
has finitely many vertices. Every such vertex has affinely independent
support: a dependence in its support would permit a nontrivial positive
and negative perturbation, contradicting extremality. In particular its
support size is at most \(r+1\). Form a matrix \(T_P\) with the rows
\(e_z-\lambda\) for all these vertices and all \(z\), omitting zero rows.
Every member of \(R_z\) is a convex combination of its vertices, so
\[
 \mathcal L(P)=\ker T_P. \tag{4}
\]

## 2. Hollow and nonhollow projections

If \(Q\) has an integer point in its relative interior, it is itself
integer-anchored. Lemma 1 then gives
\[
 \mathcal L(P)=\mathcal A(P). \tag{5}
\]
For hollow \(Q\), only proper faces impose constraints. This need not
create a nonaffine mode: a lattice simplex containing only its vertices,
for example, has \(N=r+1\) and still satisfies (5).

For a hollow two-dimensional lattice polygon with \(v\) vertices,
\(\mathcal L(P)\) has dimension exactly \(v\). All integer points lie on
the edges. The values at the polygon vertices may be assigned freely;
on each edge all other integer values are then its affine interpolation.
Lemma 1 proves both necessity and sufficiency. Thus a hollow polygon
with at least four vertices has genuine nonaffine recession modes.

For the binary square \(P=\{0,1\}^2\), every point is a vertex, so
\(\mathcal L(P)=\mathbb R^4\). The function \(g(z_1,z_2)=z_1z_2\)
belongs to this space but is not affine. The four-point affine dependence
\(g(0,0)+g(1,1)-g(1,0)-g(0,1)\) is unconstrained: its positive and
negative barycenters meet at a noninteger index. This illustrates why
one must use the anchored-face equations rather than all affine
dependencies of \(P\).

In all dimensions restriction from \(\mathcal L(P)\) to the vertices of
\(Q\) is injective. Indeed a point \(z\in P\) lies in the relative
interior of its integer-anchored minimal face, where its value is affine
interpolation of that face's vertex values. The allowable vertex values
are precisely those affine on the vertices of each integer-anchored
face. Their extensions agree on intersecting faces because affine
functions agreeing at that intersection's vertices agree throughout
the intersection.

## 3. The exact translation symmetry of fiber compatibility

Let nonempty compact convex sets \(K_z\subset\mathbb R^d\), \(z\in P\),
be the actual integer fibers of
\[
 C=\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{z\in P}(\{z\}\times K_z).
\]
Equivalently, for every representation in (1),
\[
 \sum_w\lambda_w K_w\subset K_z. \tag{6}
\]
To see sufficiency, any point of the convex hull at index \(z\) has a
representation using one point per source fiber, after aggregating
terms with the same source index. Equation (6) places it in \(K_z\).

If \(h:P\to\mathbb R^d\) has every coordinate in \(\mathcal L(P)\), then
the translated family \(K_z+h(z)\) also satisfies (6): its Minkowski sum
at any representation is
\[
 \sum_w\lambda_w(K_w+h(w))
     =\sum_w\lambda_w K_w+h(z)\subset K_z+h(z). \tag{7}
\]
Conversely, if the singleton family \(\{h(z)\}\) is actual, (6) says
exactly that the coordinates of \(h\) lie in \(\mathcal L(P)\).
The same necessity follows by testing translations of one common
nonempty compact convex body \(K\): a nonzero translation of \(K\)
cannot be contained in \(K\), as an exposing linear functional in the
translation direction shows.

Thus \(\mathcal L(P)\otimes\mathbb R^d\) is the exact vector space of
fiber translations preserving every actual family over \(P\).
Only its ordinary affine subspace is an ambient affine shear.
Translations by a nonaffine member preserve fiber compatibility but
need not send ambient halfspaces to halfspaces; they do not give a
depth-preserving normalization.

## 4. Bounded diameters force all divergence into this space

Consider a sequence of actual families \(K_{j,z}\), with
\[
 \operatorname{diam}K_{j,z}\le D<\infty
                  \quad\hbox{for all }j,z. \tag{8}
\]
Choose \(c_j(z)\in K_{j,z}\). In particular one can use the ordinary
centroid when the fiber has positive \(d\)-volume, or its centroid in
its affine hull otherwise. Only membership is needed below.

For any representation \(\lambda\in R_z\), convexity gives
\(\sum_w\lambda_wc_j(w)\in K_{j,z}\). Therefore
\[
 \left|c_j(z)-\sum_w\lambda_wc_j(w)\right|\le D. \tag{9}
\]

Let \(m\) be the number of nonzero rows of \(T_P\) from (4), and give
arrays the Euclidean/Frobenius norm. Applying (9) row by row yields
\[
 \|T_Pc_j\|_F\le D\sqrt m. \tag{10}
\]
If \(T_P\ne0\), let \(\sigma_P>0\) be its least positive singular value.
The orthogonal complement of its kernel has all singular values at
least \(\sigma_P\); hence
\[
 \operatorname{dist}\bigl(c_j,\mathcal L(P)\otimes\mathbb R^d\bigr)
       \le\frac{D\sqrt m}{\sigma_P}. \tag{11}
\]
If \(T_P=0\), the distance is zero. This is a uniform quantitative
statement, not merely a subsequential assertion.

To formulate divergence modulo ordinary affine shears, let \(a_j\)
be the orthogonal projection of the centroid array onto
\(\mathcal A(P)\otimes\mathbb R^d\), and suppose
\[
 R_j:=\|c_j-a_j\|_F\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Set \(h_j=(c_j-a_j)/R_j\). The finite-dimensional unit sphere is compact,
so along a subsequence \(h_j\to h\), with \(\|h\|_F=1\). Affine arrays
annihilate every row of \(T_P\), so (10) gives
\[
 T_Ph=\lim_j T_Ph_j=0.
\]
Furthermore each \(h_j\) is orthogonal to the ordinary affine arrays.
Thus
\[
 0\ne h\in
 (\mathcal L(P)\otimes\mathbb R^d)
 \cap(\mathcal A(P)\otimes\mathbb R^d)^\perp. \tag{12}
\]
This proves that every normalized diverging centroid mode after best
ordinary affine shears belongs to the claimed recession space. For a
nonhollow projection, (5) and (12) rule out such divergence altogether.

## 5. Exact induced graph and its convexity space

For any vector-valued \(h\) with coordinates in \(\mathcal L(P)\), put
\[
 G_h=\operatorname{conv}\{(z,h(z)):z\in P\},\qquad
 \Gamma_h=\{(z,h(z)):z\in P\}.
\]
The projection of \(G_h\) is \(Q\). At an integer index, lattice convexity
forces \(z\in P\), and (1) forces every representation of that index to
have continuous coordinate \(h(z)\). Therefore
\[
 G_h\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)=\Gamma_h. \tag{13}
\]
Each fiber is exactly a singleton, even if \(G_h\) has much higher affine
dimension than \(Q\). In particular its intrinsic mixed dimension is zero.

There is a stronger identity for every subset \(A\subset P\):
\[
 \Gamma_h\cap\operatorname{conv}\{(z,h(z)):z\in A\}
 =\{(z,h(z)):z\in P\cap\operatorname{conv}A\}. \tag{14}
\]
Projection gives one inclusion; (1) applied to a representation using
\(A\) gives the other.

Consequently the finite convexity spaces on \(P\) and \(\Gamma_h\) are
isomorphic. Explicitly, a subset of either finite set is the trace of
a closed convex set if and only if it equals its relative convex hull
closure. Equation (14) identifies these closures. Conversely each
closed subset is realized by its own finite convex hull. Thus the
relative Helly numbers are exactly equal:
\[
 h(\Gamma_h)=h(P). \tag{15}
\]
This asserts equality for convex-set traces, not equality of their
halfspace traces; a nonlinear lift can create additional halfspace
separations.

## 6. The weighted graph centerpoint bound

The affine lattice \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^n\) has rank \(r\):
after choosing an origin in \(P\), a lattice basis identifies it affinely
with \(\mathbb Z^r\). This identification concerns only the affine
projection space and does not apply an untracked transformation to the
continuous fibers. Doignon's theorem in that lattice gives
\[
 h(P)\le2^r.
\]
For completeness, insert the fixed convex set \(Q\) along with any family
whose intersection misses \(P\); their intersection misses the whole
affine lattice, so at most \(2^r\) of the sets suffice. Dropping the fixed
set from the selected count still leaves at most \(2^r\) original sets.
Also \(h(P)\le N\): from an infeasible family choose, for each point of
\(P\), one set excluding it. When \(r=0\), the assertions are simply
\(h(P)=1\).

Let
\[
 \nu=\sum_{z\in P}w_z\delta_{(z,h(z))},\qquad
 w_z\ge0,\quad W=\sum_z w_z>0.
\]
Then there exists a single \(y\in\Gamma_h\) such that **every closed
ambient halfspace** containing \(y\) satisfies
\[
 \nu(H)\ge\frac{W}{h(P)}
       \ge\frac{W}{\min(N,2^r)}. \tag{16}
\]

Here is a proof that includes atoms. Normalize \(W=1\), and put
\(h_0=h(P)\). Consider all closed halfspaces of measure greater than
\(1-1/h_0\). Any at most \(h_0\) of these have intersection of positive
measure, by the union bound on their complements. The Helly property
(15), and then the finite intersection property on the finite set
\(\Gamma_h\), give a point belonging to all of them. If a closed
halfspace \(H\) through or containing this point had measure below
\(1/h_0\), its open complementary halfspace would have measure greater
than \(1-1/h_0\). Because the support is finite, a closed halfspace
strictly inside that open complement can retain all its support points.
It would be one of the chosen high-mass halfspaces while excluding the
selected point, a contradiction. This proves (16), with all boundary
atoms counted as required.

## 6a. A universal lift bounds the dimension of the recession space

There is an additional bound independent of the number of projection
points:
\[
 \boxed{\ \dim\mathcal L(P)\le h(P)\le\min(N,2^r).\ } \tag{20}
\]
Here is a complete proof of the first inequality. Write
\(\ell=\dim\mathcal L(P)\), choose a basis
\(1,g_1,\ldots,g_{\ell-1}\) of this space, and define
\[
 \Phi(z)=(g_1(z),\ldots,g_{\ell-1}(z)).
\]
The affine span of \(\Phi(P)\) has dimension exactly \(\ell-1\). Otherwise
an affine equation on this image would be a nontrivial linear relation
among the displayed basis functions. Each original coordinate function
\(z_i\) belongs to \(\mathcal A(P)\subset\mathcal L(P)\), so there is an
affine map \(\pi_0\) with \(\pi_0(\Phi(z))=z\) for every \(z\in P\).
In particular \(\Phi\) is injective.

For every \(A\subset P\), projection by \(\pi_0\) and then (1) show
\[
 \Phi(P)\cap\operatorname{conv}\Phi(A)
      =\Phi(P\cap\operatorname{conv}A).
\]
Thus the same proof as (15) gives \(h(\Phi(P))=h(P)\). If desired one
can retain explicit integer coordinates and use
\(\widetilde\Phi(z)=(z,\Phi(z))\): its extra coordinates are affine
functions of \(\Phi(z)\), so it has the same affine dimension and is
affinely isomorphic to \(\Phi(P)\). It is an actual singleton-fiber
mixed graph by (13). This avoids treating an arbitrary feature
coordinate as an integer coordinate.

Every finite set of affine dimension \(D\) has relative Helly number at
least \(D+1\). Choose \(D+1\) affinely independent points in the set and
take the \(D+1\) closed facets of their simplex as test convex sets. Any
at most \(D\) facets intersect at one of the chosen vertices, whereas all
\(D+1\) facets have empty intersection. For \(D=0\), use the elementary
fact that a nonempty finite set has Helly number at least one. Applying
this to \(\Phi(P)\) proves \(h(P)\ge\ell\), and hence (20).

Consequently the scalar nonaffine recession space has dimension at most
\[
 2^r-r-1,
\]
and the vector-valued space of modes modulo ordinary shears has dimension
at most \(d(2^r-r-1)\). The bound controls the number of independent modes;
it does not bound their size or authorize removing them by a nonlinear
depth-preserving map.

Some exact equality cases and limitations are immediate:

* For \(r=0\), \(\ell=1\), and for \(r=1\), \(\ell=2\).
* For \(r\ge2\), equality \(\ell=2^r\) forces \(Q\) to be hollow, since
  otherwise \(\ell=r+1<2^r\).
* In dimension two, the hollow-polygon calculation in Section 2 and
  (20) show that every hollow lattice polygon has at most four vertices.
  Moreover \(\ell=4\) holds exactly for the hollow quadrilaterals.
* Equality does not bound \(N\). For
  \(P=\{0,1,\ldots,m\}\times\{0,1\}\), \(m\ge1\), the two rows impose
  separate affine interpolations, so \(\ell=4\) for all \(m\). The
  universal hull is a tetrahedron; additional integer points map to
  points on two opposite edges.

There is also an exact recursion in the width-one class. If the only
integer heights of \(P\subset\mathbb Z^{r-1}\times\mathbb Z\) are zero
and one, let \(P_0,P_1\) be its nonempty layer projections. Every convex
representation of an integer point in one layer uses only that layer.
Therefore
\[
 \mathcal L(P)=\mathcal L(P_0)\oplus\mathcal L(P_1),\qquad
 \dim\mathcal L(P)=\dim\mathcal L(P_0)+\dim\mathcal L(P_1). \tag{21}
\]
If \(P\) has rank \(r\), (20) applied in the two layers proves that
equality \(\dim\mathcal L(P)=2^r\) holds precisely when both layers have
rank \(r-1\) and dimension \(2^{r-1}\) of their respective \(\mathcal L\)
spaces. This characterizes equality within this width-one class. No
classification of all higher-dimensional hollow equality cases is
asserted here.

## 7. What the collapse proves, and what it loses

Extend each ordinary affine array \(a_j\) to an affine map on
\(\mathbb R^n\), and apply
\[
 (z,x)\longmapsto (z,(x-a_j(z))/R_j). \tag{17}
\]
For each finite \(j\), this is an invertible ambient affine map preserving
\(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d\). It multiplies every fiber's
\(d\)-volume by the same factor \(R_j^{-d}\), so normalized depth is
unchanged when using mixed \(d\)-volume. The sheared and contracted fibers
lie within distance \(D/R_j\) of \(h_j(z)\). They therefore converge
simultaneously in Hausdorff distance to the singleton fibers of (13),
and their convex hulls converge to \(G_h\).

If the normalized original fiber masses are \(p_{j,z}\), pass to a
subsequence with \(p_{j,z}\to p_z\). Denote by \(\mu_j\) the pushforwards
of the normalized mixed measures under (17). They converge weakly to
\[
 \nu=\sum_{z\in P}p_z\delta_{(z,h(z))}. \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, each contracted fiber has diameter tending to zero and lies at
its convergent graph point, so a continuous test function has uniformly
vanishing oscillation on each fiber. Summing the finitely many weighted
oscillations proves the claim. Some \(p_z\) may be zero. Formula (18)
usually is **not** normalized counting measure on \(\Gamma_h\), although
the intrinsic Hausdorff measure of that graph is counting measure.

More precisely, consider halfspaces through candidate points
\(y_j\to y=(z_*,h(z_*))\), with normalized normals
\((a_j,b_j)\to(a,b)\ne0\). Define
\[
 L(z)=a\cdot(z-z_*)+b\cdot(h(z)-h(z_*)).
\]
All fibers with \(L(z)>0\) eventually lie wholly inside, and all fibers
with \(L(z)<0\) eventually lie wholly outside. Thus
\[
 \sum_{L(z)>0}p_z
 \le\liminf_j\mu_j(H_j)
 \le\limsup_j\mu_j(H_j)
 \le\sum_{L(z)\ge0}p_z. \tag{19}
\]
The fibers with \(L(z)=0\) are unresolved by the first scale. Their
limiting graph atoms are counted fully by the closed limiting halfspace,
whereas the original halfspaces can cut their continuous mass. Their
bounded shapes, lower-order displacements, and lower-order changes in
the normal determine that missing contribution.

There is no inference from (16) alone to a corresponding original depth.
Even a contracting single simplex has unchanged normalized maximum depth
\(\gamma_d\), while its atomic point limit has depth one. An example
with an actual nonaffine divergent mode is \(P=\{0,1\}^2\),
\(h(z)=z_1z_2 e_1\), and
\[
 K_{j,z}=j h(z)+K
\]
for a fixed \(d\)-simplex \(K\), \(d\ge1\). Every projection point is
extreme, so these are exact fibers. Each centroid has depth at least
\(\gamma_d/4\) from its own fiber. For any candidate, a simplex cap
through that candidate retaining at most \(\gamma_d\) of its own fiber
can be isolated from the other fibers by a sufficiently strong integer
normal exposing its binary index. Hence the original maximum is exactly
\(\gamma_d/4\). After subtracting the best affine shear and dividing by
the diverging residual norm, the graph limit still has four projection
vertices of equal weight, and its maximum atomic depth is exactly
\(1/4\). The difference is precisely boundary mass lost at the collapsed
fiber scale.

Finally, a boundary index set \(B=\{z\in P:L(z)=0\}\) is lattice-convex:
if an integer point belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}B\), it belongs to
\(P\), and (1) makes its value of \(L\) zero. This identifies legitimate
next-scale index sets. It does not guarantee reduced integer dimension,
reduced continuous dimension, adequate mass in a chosen set, or a common
point controlling all such boundary sets. Those additional steps remain
separate from this recession-space and graph analysis.
